headline: Sure silver for sepak takraw women’s doubles
snippet: NAGOYA, Japan – The Philippines is now assured of another silver medal – potentially a gold if stars align – as the courageous sepak takraw women’s doubles squad continued its wondrous campaign at the 20th Asian Games Aichi-Nagoya 2026. On another rainy Monday, Sept. 28, the women’s crew of Nelly Jay Salon, Jean Marie Sucalit and Abegail Sinogbuhan overwhelmed Laos, 15-12, 15-10, in their semis match at the Mizuho Park Athletic Gymnasium. It was a remarkable win for the sepak takraw team, whose two-game winning run in the preliminary round was cut short by South Korea, 1-2, earlier in the day. Since it was a no-bearing match, they took the loss positively. True enough, against Laotian bets, they were precise and entertaining, what with their acrobatic kicks and rock-hard defense. But the men’s squad of Jayson Huerte, Jom Rafael, Rey Asilum, Glindil Phori, and Ronsited Gabayeron was not lucky enough, falling to Malaysian in riveting semis, 15-10, 11-15, 7-15, to settle for the bronze. Still, it was enough for the sepak takraw squad to eclipse its two-bronze medal haul in the Hangzhou Games three years ago. In the finals, the Filipinas will face Vietnam, which defeated South Korea, 15-6, 15-13, in the other semis match. Despite the latest bronze, Team Philippines remained in 16th place with two golds, two silver and 10 bronze medals at 4 p.m., with China enjoying the view atop the medal standings with 126 golds followed by Japan (39) and South Korea (21). For sure, there will be more good news to come heading to the final five days of this sporting spectacle among 45 countries. Tennis phenom Alex Eala is still playing against a Thai opponent as off press time, but she is expected to march into the next round, owing to her stellar resume. Olympians Nesthy Petecio and Carlo Paalam were scheduled to fight late Monday afternoon, with both boxers eyeing a semis berth that will guarantee a bronze medal each. However, they will be fighting against equally dangerous Chinese opponents. After two bronze medal finishes, PH officials and its adoring fans back home hope to finally win the ultimate prize in an esports event as Sibol’s Mobile Legends: Bang Bang squad begins its highly anticipated campaign at the Aichi Sky Expo in Japan on Tuesday, Sept. 29. Sibol earlier lost to China in the semifinals of the Honor of Kings event, which was expected anyway given China’s immense status. Despite the pressure as high as Mount Fuji, the Sibol squad is heavily favored to claim the gold medal in the Land of the Rising Sun starting with their game against Jordan in Group C at 2 p.m. and Kazakhstan at 5 p.m. on Tuesday. Well, they are not world champions in Mobile Legends for nothing. “There’s always going to be pressure, especially when people have high expectations of you. Being on top has all these expectations. We just have to stay grounded in our values and focus on our daily progress,” said Sibol coach Allec Alvarado. Karl “KarlTzy” Nepomuceno, inarguably the greatest Mobile Legends player of all time, is expected to lead the charge, along with Sanford “Sanford” Vinuya, Alston “Sanji” Pabico, Dave “Teddy” Viana, and Jaypee “Jaypee” Gonzales, and Duane “Kelra” Pillas. headline: Staff shortage hits special needs diagnostic centres
snippet: SAVANNA-LA-MAR, Westmoreland — Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon has highlighted a critical staffing shortage plaguing special needs diagnostic centres in the education sector, noting that a lack of qualified professionals persists even as the Government expands facilities to meet growing demand. “You can’t have a diagnostic centre and have no staff, and that is one of the big challenges that we face. We’re diagnosing more, and we still have to do a lot more work because there’s a long waitlist for our children who need to be assessed, and we just don’t have enough people in Jamaica,” argued Morris Dixon as she addressed a ground-breaking ceremony for the Savanna-la-Mar Inclusive High School in Westmoreland last Thursday. To combat the shortage, the Ministry of Education has implemented targeted scholarships in educational and clinical psychology for teachers wishing to specialise in these areas. However, the initiative has met an unexpected roadblock: the take-up is low. “Every opportunity I get a mic [microphone], I say it again: The Ministry of Education has scholarships for teachers who want to specialise in special needs and those areas,” stressed the minister. She pointed to a similar response to one category of the Barry Wint Scholarship being offered through the Ministry of Health and Wellness in the areas of speech therapy and occupational therapy. “Those, too, are undersubscribed,” revealed Morris Dixon. “I feel quite sad when I know the needs that we have and then we put scholarships and then they don’t get taken up,” she added. General information provided on the ministry’s website for the Master’s Degree scholarship has indicated that recipients will be bonded to work in Jamaica for a period not exceeding five years. Continuance of the award is subject to the successful candidates’ satisfactory performance in maintaining a B average or a grade point average of 3.0. Morris Dixon urged young people who have an interest in teaching to consider focusing on special education. “This is a good area for you to specialise in. It is an area where there is a tremendous need. Anyone who says they want to be a teacher you know that they intrinsically want to help children. These are children that need a lot of support, and we’re just sweetening the pot by saying there are scholarships available. Anybody who wants to go down this road, it is an area that’s just going to get even bigger and [there will be] a greater need for it. It’s an important area,” argued Morris Dixon. The education ministry is currently strengthening its capacity for diagnosis and intervention of children with significant specialist needs. This is being done through the implementation of early identification, assessment, and intervention centres across the country. Services are currently available from centres at Sam Sharpe Teachers’ College in St James and Mico University College in Kingston. The next centre to be opened will be at the College of Agriculture, Science and Education (CASE) in Portland.

headline: 'Collision course': Experts warn Trump’s 'last refuge' is his most dangerous
snippet: President Donald Trump is “ lashing out ” as he increasingly finds his influence waning — and, according to experts and historians who spoke with the Guardian, he’s never been more dangerous. The Guardian, in an article published early Saturday, described Trump’s verbal attack on CNN’s Kaitlan Collins this week as “a reminder that even Trump, who has expanded executive power and dominated the national consciousness, finds some things beyond his control .” “Indeed, 20 months into his second term, there is a widening gap between the president’s self-perceived invincibility and the reality of his waning influence,” David Smith wrote. According to Smith, “For the first time since his improbable political resurrection, Trump’s aura of authority is fading.” Former Republican strategist Rick Wilson noted this is “the beginning of the end” for Trump. “This is the decline,” Wilson said. “As powerful and transgressive as he’s been, the country does not have a positive outlook right now. In fact, the negativity and pessimism among voters has reached a point that is unparalleled since Jimmy Carter.” As Smith wrote, Wilson also compared the “current mood” among the Republican-led Congress “to a wildlife documentary.” “It needs a David Attenborough voiceover,” Wilson told the Guardian. “It’s like the gazelles wandering the savannah. … The risk factor that they face now is Trump.” Wilson argued that voters are catching on to the president’s cascading policy failures . “It’s reached the point where the magic doesn’t work any more,” Wilson said. “There’s no political upside from a president who is at 29 percent approval rating in some polls, has presided over a disastrous war, and has ended up raising energy prices and food prices – all the things that they can’t spin away." “The voters now have very much put that together. They associate the war with Trump. They associate the gas prices with Trump. They associate the grocery prices with Trump.” He added. Wilson said the more Trump “becomes a liability, the more he acts out” — and his actions threaten the Republican Party as a whole. “Everything was handed to him for a decade by that party and, now that they’re paying the price, they’ve decided this has got a little too hairy,” Wilson said. As Smith reports, Trump “ has had a rough month ”: “The Federal Reserve defied him on interest rates . The Supreme Court blocked his administration’s attempt to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots for November’s midterm elections. One judge prevented him adding his name to the Kennedy Cente r … another judge blocked his ban on three news outlets from the White House grounds." According to Smith, “even Trump’s dependable power base, the Republican party, is showing cracks amid fears that he will cost them seats in November." For former Bill Clinton adviser Bill Galston, as the Republican Party focuses on finding a new leader for the post-Trump world, “nothing will drive him crazier than the shift of the spotlight away from him.” “The prospect of passing the torch, giving up the spotlight, is intensely painful for him,” Galston said. “It’s his oxygen. Will he be able to breathe, spiritually and emotionally speaking, without it?” Longtime conservative Charlie Sykes likewise argued Trump’s biggest fear is “irrelevance,” telling the Guardian the president will “rage against it as long as he can.” “The notion that he will go quietly would be incredibly naive,” Sykes said. American University history professor Allan Lichtman agreed that Trump will get more dangerous as the spotlight fades on him. “He cannot stand not being the centre of attention and that’s dangerous,” Lichtman told the Guardian. “… [W]ho knows what crazy things he might do to reassert attention on him ? And that’s frightening.” Lichtman warned that despite Republicans appearing to distance themselves from Trump, the president maintains “enormous power – and he is certainly quite willing to use that power unconstrained.” “He doesn’t care about the courts and doesn’t care about the Congress,” Lictman said. As Smith wrote, “from this perspective, Trump’s last refuge will be the unchecked use of executive authority, a politicized justice department and a sweeping pardon power.” “With nothing to lose in his final two years, he could go out all guns blazing ,” Smith wrote. “We’re headed for a collision between a lame duck who has no respect for the constitutional norms and an opposition that may have some power to hold him accountable,” Sykes explained. “The paradox is the weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets.”
